title: Control flow and the traps in it
objective: By the end of this lesson you can write the loops and conditionals C offers, and you recognise the four spelling mistakes that compile cleanly and change what your program does.

blocks.text: The shapes here are familiar from any language. What is worth your attention is that C accepts several near-misses without complaint — a stray semicolon, a missing brace, a missing break — and each one produces a program that runs and behaves differently from the one you meant to write.

blocks.caption: The forms
lines: do { ... } while (condition);       /* body runs at least once */

blocks.text: Trap 1: the semicolon that ends the statement early

blocks.caption: Both compile; neither does what it looks like
lines: if (x > 0);            /* <- this semicolon IS the if-body */
for (i = 0; i < 10; i++);       /* an empty loop that runs ten times */
printf("%d\n", i);          /* runs once, after the loop, printing 10 */

blocks.caption: Only the first statement belongs to the if
lines: log_admin_action();    /* runs whether or not authenticated */
/* Always use braces, even for one statement.
A famous TLS vulnerability came from a duplicated goto line
under an unbraced if — the second line always executed. */

blocks.title: Braces are not a style preference in C
blocks.text: Indentation means nothing to the compiler, so a line that looks like it belongs to the if simply does not. Writing braces around every body — always, even for a single statement — removes an entire class of defect, and it is why most C style guides make it a rule rather than a suggestion.
Trap 3: switch falls through without break

blocks.caption: Execution continues into the next case
lines: /* level == 1 prints BOTH low and medium. */
/* Deliberate fall-through is legitimate — mark it so readers know it was intended: */

blocks.caption: One character apart
lines: if (status = READY) { ... }    /* assigns READY, condition is its value: always true */
if (status == READY) { ... }   /* compares — what you meant */
/* -Wall warns; some people write the constant first to make it a compile error: */

blocks.text: Loop control, and the one to avoid

blocks.caption: break, continue, and goto
lines: if (items[i] == NULL) continue;   /* skip to the next iteration */
if (items[i]->done) break;        /* leave the loop entirely */
/* goto exists. In modern C it has one accepted use: */
if (!f) goto cleanup_buf;         /* single exit path for cleanup */

blocks.title: The cleanup goto is idiomatic, not a code smell
blocks.text: C has no destructors and no finally block. When a function acquires several resources, jumping forward to a single cleanup section is how kernel and library code avoids repeating free calls in every error branch — and repetition is where a forgotten free hides. Jumping backwards, or into the middle of a block, is a different matter and is rightly rare.

blocks.caption: Braces create scope
lines: int x = 2;          /* a different variable, shadowing the outer one */
/* i does not exist here — declare it outside the loop if you need it after */

blocks.title: Trigger each trap deliberately
steps: Write: if (1 > 2); printf("printed anyway\n");   then compile and run
Write an unbraced if with two indented lines under it and confirm the second always runs
Write a switch without break and watch it fall through
Write: int s = 0; if (s = 5) printf("true\n");   and read the -Wall warning
Fix each one and confirm the warnings disappear
blocks.expected: Four programs that compile and do the wrong thing, each with a compiler warning pointing at it. Seeing them once, on purpose, is what makes them visible later in someone else's code.

cheatsheet: Always brace every if/for/while body, even a single statement
A stray semicolon after if(...) or for(...) becomes the entire body
switch falls through without break — mark deliberate fall-through with a comment
if (x = 5) assigns and is always true; -Wall warns
continue skips to the next iteration; break leaves the loop
do { } while (); runs the body at least once
goto forward to a single cleanup label is idiomatic C for multi-resource functions
Braces create scope; a loop variable declared in the for header does not outlive it

choices.C: Calls do_something only when x is positive

checkpoint.explanation: Do_something() runs unconditionally. An empty statement is a valid body. The following line is simply the next statement, regardless of the condition.

checkpoint.prompt: Why do C style guides insist on braces even for a single statement?

choices.A: Braces are required by the standard
choices.B: It makes the file larger, which helps debugging
choices.C: Indentation means nothing to the compiler

checkpoint.explanation: A second indented line therefore runs unconditionally — a real vulnerability came from exactly this. The compiler reads structure, not layout. Braces make the two agree.

checkpoint.prompt: A switch case has no break. What happens?

choices.A: Execution falls into the next case
choices.C: It is a compile error unless a break is added

checkpoint.explanation: This is called 'fall-through'. Sometimes that is what you want; when it is, add a comment so the next reader knows it was intended rather than forgotten.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is a forward goto to a cleanup label accepted in C?

choices.B: It is required by the standard
choices.C: It prevents undefined behaviour in loops
choices.D: C has no destructors or finally block

checkpoint.explanation: A single cleanup path avoids repeating free calls in every error branch — where a forgotten free hides. The alternative is duplicating cleanup in each early return, which is exactly how resource leaks get introduced.
